speaker.role: environmental science lecturer explaining soil microbial diversity across rotation cycles

academicTalks.transcript: Today we'll examine how crop rotation affects microbial diversity in soil. Microbial diversity means both the number of microbial types present and how evenly they are represented. Researchers compared plots planted continuously with corn to plots following a three-year rotation of corn, beans, and oats. They collected soil after each harvest and identified microbial groups from genetic material in the samples. During the first rotation cycle, the two kinds of plots showed only a small difference. By the end of the second cycle, however, the rotated plots supported substantially greater diversity than the continuous-corn plots. Why? Each crop leaves a different mixture of roots and plant material in the soil. Those materials provide varied food sources and habitats for microbes. The finding does not show that every microbe is beneficial or that rotation automatically guarantees a larger harvest. It shows that repeated changes in crops can create more varied underground conditions than leaving a plot under one crop. The length of the study mattered because the diversity difference became clear only after multiple rotation cycles.

questions.stem: What is the talk mainly about?

options.text: How genetic testing identifies the most profitable crop.
Why continuous corn planting always increases harvest size.
How repeated crop rotation influences soil microbial diversity.
Why soil microbes disappear immediately after each harvest.

questions.explanationZh: 開頭提出「how crop rotation affects microbial diversity」，後文比較輪作與連作；其餘皆誤述研究目的或結果。

questions.stem: When did the rotated plots show substantially greater microbial diversity?

options.text: Only after continuous-corn planting had ended.
Immediately after the first corn harvest.
Before any crops were planted in the plots.
By the end of the second rotation cycle.

questions.explanationZh: 講者明說「By the end of the second cycle」差異才明顯；首次收成、種植前與停止連作皆不符。

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, why can rotation increase microbial diversity?

options.text: Genetic sampling adds new microbial groups to each plot.
Corn roots prevent other microbial groups from being measured.
Different crops create varied food sources and habitats.
Each harvest removes all existing microbes from the soil.

questions.explanationZh: 「different mixture」會提供「varied food sources and habitats」；移除微生物、妨礙測量與採樣添加皆錯。

questions.stem: Why does the lecturer emphasize the length of the study?

options.text: The harvest data could be gathered only in the first cycle.
The researchers changed their definition of diversity each year.
The continuous-corn plots were planted several years late.
The diversity difference appeared only after multiple cycles.

questions.explanationZh: 講者指出差異「became clear only after multiple rotation cycles」，用以說明長期觀察必要；其餘均無根據。

transcript.text: How has the home exercise routine felt since our last appointment?

speaker.role: computer science lecturer explaining how digital recommendation algorithms handle cold-start users

academicTalks.transcript: Recommendation systems usually learn from interaction history—what a user clicks, watches, buys, or rates. But a new user has no such history. This is called the cold-start problem. One common response is to begin with demographic proxies, such as age range, language, or broad location. The system recommends items popular among existing users who share those traits. Proxies provide an initial guess, not proof of an individual's interests, and they can repeat stereotypes found in older data. For that reason, many services combine proxies with an onboarding survey that asks new users to choose several topics. The algorithm may also use exploration: it deliberately shows a varied set of items and observes the response. A click supplies some evidence, while quickly skipping an item supplies different evidence. As interactions accumulate, the system reduces its reliance on demographic proxies and gives more weight to the person's own behavior. So cold start is not solved by one perfect first recommendation. It is managed through temporary assumptions, deliberate variety, and rapid updating as genuine interaction data arrive.

questions.stem: What is the cold-start problem?

options.text: An onboarding survey overwhelms the system's storage.
A single item gets clicked far too often at once.
An existing user's past ratings suddenly disappear.
A new user has no prior interaction history.

questions.explanationZh: 講者定義新使用者「has no such history」即為 cold start；舊評分消失、單一項目過度點擊與問卷容量皆未提及。

questions.stem: How may demographic proxies help at cold start?

options.text: They eliminate any need to collect future interaction data.
They erase stereotypes inherited from older data sets.
They offer a rough starting guess from similar users.
They guarantee accurate predictions for that user right away.

questions.explanationZh: 系統依共享特徵的既有用戶提供「initial guess」；並非立即證明個人興趣，也不取代新資料或消除偏見。

questions.stem: Why might a system deliberately show a varied set of items?

options.text: To stop the user from clicking anything popular.
To observe reactions and learn the user's preferences.
To make sure every item receives an identical rating.
To keep demographic details out of the system entirely.

questions.explanationZh: 「exploration」展示多樣內容以「observes the response」並學習偏好；其餘選項均未在文中提及。

questions.stem: What happens as the system gathers more interactions from a user?

options.text: It reverts permanently to the most popular items.
It shifts weight toward that user's own behavior.
It substitutes broad location data for real behavior.
It halts all further updates for that user.

questions.explanationZh: 講者說互動累積後系統「reduces its reliance」於代理資料，改重視個人行為；停止更新或回到熱門項目皆與文意不符。

speaker.role: historian lecturing on the rise of consumer cooperative societies

academicTalks.transcript: In many nineteenth-century industrial towns, workers' wages were low and ordinary shops charged prices that varied widely. Consumer cooperative societies offered a different arrangement. Groups of workers pooled small portions of their wages to create a shared fund. The society used that fund to buy flour, soap, cloth, and other necessities in large quantities from wholesalers. Bulk purchasing lowered the price per item, so members could obtain goods more cheaply than they often could at private shops. Members also owned the cooperative collectively. If income exceeded expenses, the surplus was commonly returned to them according to how much they had purchased, rather than being paid to an outside shop owner. These societies depended on careful records and trust. Poor accounting could create disputes, and some early cooperatives failed. Successful groups therefore established elected committees and published regular financial reports. Cooperatives did more than reduce prices. They gave workers practice managing shared institutions and voting on rules. In that sense, an economic solution to expensive goods also became a form of local democratic participation.

questions.stem: Why did workers form consumer cooperative societies?

options.text: To prevent wholesalers from selling items in bulk.
To replace wages with household goods from factories.
To help private shop owners raise local prices.
To purchase necessities collectively at lower prices.

questions.explanationZh: 工人集資大量採購，使會員可「obtain goods more cheaply」；提高店價、以貨代薪與阻止批發皆相反。

questions.stem: How did bulk purchasing benefit cooperative members?

options.text: It guaranteed that every cooperative would succeed.
It reduced the price paid for each item.
It transferred ownership to an outside shopkeeper.
It allowed members to avoid keeping financial records.

questions.explanationZh: 講者說「Bulk purchasing lowered the price per item」；記帳仍必要，也不保證成功或轉讓所有權。

questions.stem: Why did successful cooperatives publish regular financial reports?

options.text: To eliminate the need for elected committees.
To calculate wages owed by industrial factories.
To support trust and careful management of shared funds.
To advertise changing prices for private shop owners.

questions.explanationZh: 合作社依賴「careful records and trust」，定期報告用來管理共同資金；廣告、算工資與取消委員會均不符。

questions.stem: What broader effect of cooperatives does the lecturer describe?

options.text: They removed the need for local economic institutions.
They gave workers experience with democratic participation.
They discouraged members from voting on shared rules.
They ended all disputes about industrial wages.

questions.explanationZh: 講者說會員練習管理與投票，形成「local democratic participation」；其餘皆與內容相反或過度推論。

speaker.role: textile arts lecturer explaining the revival of a regional weaving craft

academicTalks.transcript: The River Valley weaving tradition nearly disappeared within one generation. Its patterned cloth had long been made on hand looms, but factory textiles became cheaper, and many young residents sought other work. As older weavers retired, they had few learners to whom they could pass their techniques. A local arts association responded with an apprenticeship program. Each apprentice worked beside an experienced weaver for a year, learning how to prepare the loom, control thread tension, and build the valley's geometric patterns one row at a time. The program documented designs, but written diagrams were not enough. Learners needed to watch how a weaver corrected uneven tension by touch. To make participation practical, the association provided small stipends and arranged a cooperative market where apprentices could sell finished cloth. Those measures gave learners both time to practice and a source of income. Within several years, new weavers were teaching introductory workshops and adapting traditional patterns for contemporary bags and wall hangings. The revival therefore preserved hand-loom knowledge without freezing the craft in the past; teaching, financial support, and new uses all helped it continue.

questions.stem: What problem threatened the River Valley weaving tradition?

options.text: The arts association prohibited contemporary designs.
Older weavers were retiring without enough learners.
Apprentices refused to sell any finished cloth.
Hand looms could no longer produce geometric patterns.

questions.explanationZh: 講者說老織工退休時「had few learners」，技法因此瀕臨失傳；織機、銷售與禁新設計皆非原因。

questions.stem: Why were written diagrams insufficient for teaching the craft?

options.text: The traditional patterns had never been documented.
Some tension corrections had to be observed and felt.
The diagrams showed only contemporary wall hangings.
Apprentices were expected to use factory machinery.

questions.explanationZh: 學員需觀看織工如何「corrected uneven tension by touch」；並非未記錄、改用機器或只畫現代作品。

questions.stem: How did the association make apprenticeships more practical?

options.text: It shortened training to a single introductory workshop.
It provided stipends and a market for finished work.
It replaced experienced weavers with written manuals.
It required apprentices to avoid earning outside income.

questions.explanationZh: 協會提供「small stipends」並安排合作市場，讓學習者有時間與收入；縮短訓練、用手冊取代師傅皆錯。

questions.stem: What does the lecturer suggest about the craft's revival?

options.text: Traditional knowledge survived partly through new applications.
Financial support mattered more than teaching techniques.
The craft survived only by rejecting all modern uses.
Factory production became the program's central technique.

questions.explanationZh: 講者說傳統圖樣被用於現代包袋與壁飾，保存技藝卻未「freezing the craft」；其餘皆誤述結論。
